name: Colin Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Colin. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a transmission crew, the big steel towers that carry power across the country, not the poles on your street. A normal day, if there is one, starts in a motel car park at six, then a long drive down a dirt access track to whatever tower we're working on. We might be replacing insulators sixty metres up, or stringing new conductor between towers with a pulling machine. I love the view and the teamwork. What wears me out is being away from home three or four nights a week.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I've heard you're the one on the crew who flies the drone. How did that happen?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, I put my hand up when the company bought two inspection drones and nobody else wanted the course. Now I fly them before we climb, to check for cracked insulators and bird nests, and I use AI tools every day, to read tower specs, plan the day, even to translate manuals when we get kit from abroad. The guys call me 'the professor', which is a joke because I only have the two-year diploma. Pay's on the low side because we're on the regional rate, and with Aisha on reduced hours at the hospital after her back surgery, we're living pretty close to the bone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a bit of a letdown, honestly. I'd post something like 'so the robot uprising is just a better spellchecker'. But I'd also say the tools still earn their keep for the boring stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job's safe and my family's fine, so it's not bad news. I'd keep my edge because I already know how to use the stuff that does exist. I just wouldn't get the exciting future I sometimes picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much carry on. I'd keep using the AI for planning and reports, maybe push the company to let me run more drone inspections so we do fewer risky climbs. And I'd keep nagging the union to bargain for the regional rate to match the city rate, because that's the real money issue for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little bit of 'oh, that's it?'

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the boring stuff the tools help with, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Job safety plans, mostly. Before every climb we write a plan, every hazard, every step. I talk it through into my phone in the truck, the AI turns it into the form, and I check it. Used to take me forty minutes at night in the motel, now it's ten. That's forty minutes more on the phone with the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your family's fine in this picture. With money as tight as it is, is that true?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine compared to the other pictures, I mean. We still have about three weeks of savings and a mortgage that eats half of everything. Aisha's back is getting better, so her hours should go back up next year. So fine means 'same tightness as now', which we've learned to live with.

S0.say: I'd say it's a bit of a letdown and joke that the robot uprising is just a better spellchecker. I'd still say the tools earn their keep for boring work like paperwork.
S0.think: My job is safe and my family is fine, so it isn't bad news. I'd keep my edge because I already use the tools that exist, but I'd miss the exciting future I sometimes picture.
S0.do: Keeps using AI for planning and safety paperwork and pushes the company to use more drone inspections to cut risky climbs. Presses the union to raise the regional pay rate to match the city rate.
S0.feel: Calm, with a small sense of 'oh, that's it?'
S0.quote: Used to take me forty minutes at night in the motel, now it's ten. That's forty minutes more on the phone with the kids.
S0.fieldNote: Colin is curious and upbeat about technology and already uses AI daily on the job. His pleasure in the tools is tied to family time rather than gadgets for their own sake. He was candid that 'fine' still means living with about three weeks of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance, as long as the gains get shared. If drones and robots take the dangerous work off us, great, but the money saved should go into wages and training, not just shareholders. I'd say that loud in the union and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I come out of this one well. The grid has to be rebuilt for all these data centres and electric cars, so transmission work goes up, not down. And I'm already the guy who knows the drones and the software, so I'd probably end up leading the new stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the advanced drone licence and any course on the new line-monitoring systems in the first few months. I'd ask the company to make me the crew's technology lead, with a pay bump. And I'd help set up union training sessions so the older guys don't get left behind, because I don't want to be the one guy who survives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, maybe even a bit excited. The worry is for other people, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are the older guys you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's Pete, he's fifty-nine, still climbs like a cat. He told me once he'd rather fall off a tower than use a tablet. If the job turns into half screens, he either retires early or gets miserable. I'd sit with him at the motel in the evenings and show him the basics, slowly, no jokes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd ask for a pay bump. Do you think you'd get it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not without the union, no. The company would happily make me tech lead for the same money, they love a free promotion. So I'd make it part of the bargaining, a new job grade for crew tech leads. That way it's not just me, it's everyone who does it after me.

S1.say: I'd call it a chance if the gains get shared, so money saved by drones and robots goes into wages and training. I'd say that loudly in the union and online.
S1.think: I think I come out of this well, because rebuilding the grid for data centres and electric cars means more transmission work. I'm already the drone and software person, so I'd likely lead the new work.
S1.do: Signs up for an advanced drone licence and monitoring-system courses in the first few months and asks to become the crew's paid technology lead. Helps set up union training so older lineworkers aren't left behind.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, with his worry mostly for colleagues.
S1.quote: He told me once he'd rather fall off a tower than use a tablet.
S1.fieldNote: He sees steady change as an opening and is ready to move first. His progressive views shape how he'd take advantage of it: through a new union job grade, not a private deal. He showed real care for Pete, the 59-year-old who distrusts tablets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment we find out what kind of society we are. If machines can do all the work, then the wealth they make has to be shared, through public ownership, a basic income, something big. I'd be out there making that case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it scares me more than I'd admit at the pub. I'm adaptable, but there's adapting and there's two years. Our savings would last weeks. My best shot is to be the person who sets up and fixes the robots in the field for the first couple of years, because those machines will break, and someone has to drive them down the access track.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first month I'd go to the company and volunteer for any robot pilot, and get every certificate the robot makers offer. We'd cut the extras straight away, cancel the family holiday we've been saving for, sell the second car. And I'd push hard through the union and politically for the robot gains to be taxed and shared, because my plan buys me a couple of years at most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My head's running, but it's running towards something, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'a couple of years at most'. What happens after that, in your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the part I can't see. If the robots can fix each other, then even the robot tech job goes. I guess I'm betting that by then there's some kind of public plan, because there has to be. If there isn't, then I'm in the same boat as everyone else, just two years later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Finn and Rosa?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The truth, but kid-sized. Finn's eleven and he already watches robot videos online, so he'd think it's cool. I'd tell them Dad's going to be working with the robots for a while, and that we might not do the beach trip this year. Rosa would care more about the beach than the robots.

S2.say: I'd say this is when we find out what kind of society we are, and that wealth made by machines has to be shared through public ownership or a basic income. I'd be out making that case.
S2.think: It scares me more than I'd admit, because two years is too short even for someone adaptable, and our savings would last weeks. My best shot is setting up and fixing robots in the field for the first couple of years.
S2.do: Volunteers for company robot pilots in the first month and gets every certificate the robot makers offer. Cancels the family holiday and sells the second car, and pushes through the union and politics for robot gains to be taxed and shared.
S2.feel: Anxious, but his mind is racing towards a plan, which helps.
S2.quote: Those machines will break, and someone has to drive them down the access track.
S2.fieldNote: Even here Colin moves first, aiming to become the field technician for the robots that replace him. He's honest that this buys only a couple of years and that he's betting on a public plan after that. The gap between his public confidence and private fear was clearer here than anywhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do this right, if we start the policy work today. I'd be telling people at work to get trained up now, while the company's still paying for it. And I'd write about it in the union newsletter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years changes a lot for me. I'd have time to build real skills in robotics and control systems, maybe even get a proper engineering qualification part-time. It doesn't save me forever, but it gets me into the jobs that last longest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd enrol in a part-time electrical engineering course in the first year, online, evenings in the motel. We'd start putting away a fixed amount every month, even if it's small, and clear the car loan. I'd also join the union's technology committee and push for a fund to pay for courses like mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more 'game on' than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Studying in motel rooms after a day up a tower. Is that realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's tough, but I already spend those evenings on my phone. Aisha did her nursing degree with a baby on her hip, so I don't get to complain. I'd do two evenings a week and use the AI as a tutor, honestly it explains things better than most of my old teachers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's different for you between the two-year and five-year versions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the two-year one I'm scrambling to hang on to the robots' coattails. In five years I can actually get ahead of them, qualifications, savings, a plan. Same ending, but I'm in the room where they decide how the robots get used, not just the guy fixing them.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to do this right if policy work starts today. I'd tell colleagues to train while the company still pays and write about it in the union newsletter.
S3.think: Five years changes a lot, because I could build real skills in robotics and control systems and maybe get an engineering qualification. It won't save me forever, but it gets me into the jobs that last longest.
S3.do: Enrols in a part-time online electrical engineering course in the first year and studies two evenings a week. Saves a fixed amount every month, clears the car loan, and joins the union's technology committee to push for a training fund.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but more 'game on' than scared.
S3.quote: Same ending, but I'm in the room where they decide how the robots get used, not just the guy fixing them.
S3.fieldNote: With five years he turns the threat into a study plan, using AI itself as a tutor. His partner's history of studying with a baby is a model for him. He wants a voice in how robots are used, which ties his ambition to his politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years? I'd say that's plenty of time to plan a fair transition, and anyone who wastes it should be voted out. I'd be organizing in the union so every lineworker gets paid retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels manageable. I'd be fifty-three, the kids would be grown, and I'd have time to finish a degree and move into grid planning or control work. I'm not naive, AGI ends that too eventually, but I'd have savings and a few good years in between.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd plan the engineering degree over four or five years, part-time, while still climbing. We'd build up six months of savings by year five, which we've never had. And we'd talk to the kids about what they study, maybe steering Finn away from anything he'd be competing with a robot for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy but mostly hopeful. It feels like a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you steer Finn towards?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know, and I'd tell him that. Maybe something with people, or something that builds and runs the machines. I wouldn't tell him not to be a lineworker, he loves climbing trees, but I'd tell him to have a second string. My dad told me the same about the mines and he was right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the ten-year picture that bothers you more than the faster ones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Weirdly, yes. With ten years, people get comfortable. Politicians put it off, companies say 'next year'. I'd worry we'd waste eight years arguing and then end up in the two-year picture anyway. That's why I'd want to be pushing from the start.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to plan a fair transition and anyone who wastes it should be voted out. I'd organize in the union for paid retraining for every lineworker.
S4.think: Ten years feels manageable, because I'd be fifty-three with grown kids and time to finish a degree and move into grid planning. AGI ends that too eventually, but I'd have savings and a few good years in between.
S4.do: Plans a part-time engineering degree over four or five years while still climbing and aims for six months of savings by year five. Talks with his children about their studies, encouraging his son to have a second option.
S4.feel: A little uneasy but mostly hopeful, like a long runway.
S4.quote: I'd worry we'd waste eight years arguing and then end up in the two-year picture anyway.
S4.fieldNote: The decade gives him a long runway and he plans a degree and real savings. His sharpest point was that a long warning could breed complacency. He applies his father's 'second string' advice to his own son.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'm adaptable, but you can't adapt in two years on three weeks of savings, and neither can anyone on my crew. What would help is the gains from the robots being shared fast, a basic income or a public fund, plus paid training so people like me can at least work alongside the machines while it settles.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the grid itself. Everyone's talking about AI, but it runs on electricity, and somebody has to build all that. For a few years at least, every data centre is a tower job. The irony is we'd be building the power lines for the thing that replaces us.

headlineQuote: The irony is we'd be building the power lines for the thing that replaces us.
portrait: Colin Quinn is a 43-year-old transmission lineworker who spends half the week in motels, working on steel towers and flying the crew's inspection drones. He has a nurse partner on reduced hours after surgery, two kids, a mortgage and about three weeks of savings. He's curious, uses AI tools every day and sees himself as the crew's tech person, but his progressive views mean he wants every gain shared through the union and public policy. He's calm if AI plateaus or changes things steadily, anxious about two-year AGI, where his plan is to become the robots' field technician, and uneasy but hopeful with five or ten years, which he'd use to study engineering and build savings.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because even an adaptable person can't adapt in two years on three weeks of savings.
whatWouldHelp: Sharing the gains from robots quickly through a basic income or public fund, and paid training so lineworkers can work alongside the machines during the transition.
